title: Density, pressure and buoyancy
blurb: Use density to predict floating and sinking, calculate pressure from force and area and from depth, and apply Pascal's and Archimedes' principles.
question: A hydraulic dental chair lifts a patient when a small pump piston is pressed. Why does a small force raise a heavy chair, why does water pressure rise as a diver goes deeper, and why does a steel ship float?

teach.body: Formally, density is mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V, in kg/m³ or g/cm³ (1 g/cm³ = 1 g/mL). Water's density is 1,000 kg/m³, the same as 1.0 g/cm³. In plain English: density is how tightly packed the matter is. An object less dense than a fluid floats in it; a denser object sinks. A 250 g stone with a volume of 100 cm³ has ρ = 2.5 g/cm³, so it sinks in water.

Pressure P = F ÷ A, in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m²). The same force on a smaller area gives a greater pressure: a needle tip, a sharp knife, a high heel. A larger area spreads the force and lowers the pressure: snowshoes, a wide stretcher strap. Pressure is not the same thing as force; a gentle touch on a tiny area can make a large pressure.

Fluid pressure increases with depth: P = ρgh (plus the atmospheric pressure on the surface). At a given depth it pushes equally in all directions and does not depend on the container's shape or total volume. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1 atm = 101 kPa = 760 mmHg, and it is lower at altitude. Gauge pressure, such as blood pressure or tire pressure, is the pressure above atmospheric.

teach.h: Extra pressure vs depth in fresh water (g = 10 m/s²)
teach.caption: A straight line: double the depth, double the extra pressure. Every 10 m of water adds about one atmosphere.

teach.h: Pascal's principle in a hydraulic lift
teach.caption: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂. Hydraulic lifts and brakes multiply force, not energy: work in = work out.

teach.body: A fluid pushes up on anything in it with a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced. If the buoyant force on a fully submerged object exceeds its weight, it rises; if less, it sinks. A floating object displaces exactly its own weight of fluid, and the fraction below the surface equals ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid. A steel ship floats because its hollow shape displaces a huge volume of water. Bernoulli: where a fluid flows faster, its pressure is lower.

teach.h: Scenario: Mateo and the dental chair
teach.body: Mateo, a dental hygiene applicant, learns how the hydraulic chair works. A 50 N push on a 0.0020 m² pump piston creates a pressure of 25,000 Pa. Pascal's principle carries it to a 0.10 m² lift piston: F₂ = 25,000 × 0.10 = 2,500 N, enough to raise the chair and patient. The pump piston must travel 50 times as far as the chair rises, so the work in still equals the work out.

teach.text: Pressure is not force: a larger area LOWERS pressure. Fluid pressure depends on depth, density and g, not on the container's shape or volume. The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced; it equals the object's weight only when the object floats. Hydraulics multiply force, never energy. Faster flow means LOWER pressure (Bernoulli).

items: ρ = m/V; water = 1,000 kg/m³ = 1.0 g/cm³; less dense floats, denser sinks.
P = F/A in pascals; smaller area, greater pressure.
Fluid pressure P = ρgh rises with depth, acts in all directions, ignores container shape.
Pascal: F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ (more force, less distance).
Archimedes: buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced; fraction submerged = ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid.

summary: You can now calculate density and predict whether an object floats, and calculate pressure from force and area and from depth in a fluid. You can also use Pascal's principle for hydraulic systems and Archimedes' principle for buoyant force and the fraction of a floating object below the surface.

A.q: Which of these is equal to one pascal?
A.why: Pressure = force ÷ area, so 1 Pa = 1 newton per square meter.

whyNot.0: 1 N·m is a joule, the unit of work (or torque).
whyNot.1: kg/m³ is a unit of density.
whyNot.3: 1 J/s is a watt, the unit of power.

A.q: A 400 g object has a volume of 500 cm³. What is its density, and will it float in water (1.0 g/cm³)?
A.why: ρ = m/V = 400 ÷ 500 = 0.80 g/cm³. That is less than water's 1.0 g/cm³, so it floats.

whyNot.1: Inverts the formula (500 ÷ 400); density is mass ÷ volume.
whyNot.2: Inverts the formula, and a density above 1.0 g/cm³ would sink.
whyNot.3: The density is right, but an object less dense than water floats.

A.q: Why do snowshoes keep a hiker from sinking into deep snow?
options: They spread the force, lowering pressure
They add buoyant force from the snow
A.why: P = F/A. The hiker's weight is unchanged, but spreading it over a larger area lowers the pressure on the snow.

whyNot.0: The hiker weighs the same; the area changes.
whyNot.2: Snowshoes increase the area, which lowers the pressure.
whyNot.3: Snow does not hold a hiker up by buoyancy; lower pressure is the reason.

B.q: A 500 N crate rests on a base with an area of 0.25 m². What pressure does it exert on the floor?

whyNot.3: Gives the force value as the pressure; it must be divided by the area.

B.q: A diver feels more pressure the deeper she swims in a lake. What determines the water pressure at a given depth?
options: The total volume of the lake
The shape of the lake bed
The surface area of the lake
The depth, water density and g
B.why: Fluid pressure P = ρgh depends on density, g and depth, not on the size or shape of the body of water.

whyNot.0: A small pond and a huge lake give the same pressure at the same depth.
whyNot.1: Container shape does not change pressure at a given depth.
whyNot.2: Surface area does not change pressure at a given depth.

B.q: A 30 N object is held fully under water, where it displaces 12 N of water. What is the buoyant force, and what happens when it is released?
B.why: Buoyant force = weight of water displaced = 12 N. That is less than its 30 N weight, so it sinks.

whyNot.0: The buoyant force is the displaced water's weight (12 N), not the object's weight.
whyNot.1: The buoyant force is right, but 12 N up is less than 30 N down.
whyNot.3: 18 N is the net downward force (30 − 12), not the buoyant force.

C.q: A hydraulic jack has a 0.0050 m² input piston and a 0.25 m² output piston. What input force lifts a 10,000 N car? (F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂)

whyNot.1: Inverts the area ratio; the small piston needs the smaller force.
whyNot.2: Multiplies by A₁ but forgets to divide by A₂.

C.q: A block floats in fresh water with 40% of its volume below the surface. What is the block's density? (ρ_water = 1,000 kg/m³)
C.why: Fraction submerged = ρ_object ÷ ρ_fluid, so ρ_object = 0.40 × 1,000 = 400 kg/m³.

whyNot.0: Uses the 60% above the surface instead of the 40% below.
whyNot.1: Divides by the fraction (1,000 ÷ 0.40) instead of multiplying.
whyNot.2: A block with water's density would float fully submerged, not 40% under.

C.q: What extra pressure does seawater exert on a diver 20 m below the surface? Use ρ = 1,030 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s².

whyNot.3: Adds a ½ that does not belong in ρgh.

reteach.title: Climbing into a full bathtub
reteach.question: Why does the water level rise when you climb into a bath, and why do you feel lighter?

blocks.h: You push water out of the way
blocks.body: Your body takes up space that water used to fill, so the water is pushed aside and the level rises: that pushed-aside water is the displaced fluid. The water pushes back up on you with a force equal to the weight of the water you displaced. That upward push is the buoyant force, which is why your arm floats up and you feel lighter. Sink lower and you displace more water, so the push grows.

blocks.text: The buoyant force depends on the fluid displaced, not on what the object is made of. Two objects of the same size fully under water feel the same buoyant force.

explain.body: Compute ρ = m/V, then compare with the fluid. Water is 1.0 g/cm³.

test.q: A 90 g ring has a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density, and does it float in water?
test.why: ρ = 90 ÷ 10 = 9.0 g/cm³, far more than water's 1.0 g/cm³, so it sinks.

whyNot.1: The density is right, but a denser object sinks.
whyNot.2: Multiplies mass by volume instead of dividing.

explain.body: Divide the force by a very small area and the pressure becomes very large.

test.q: A 600 N weight rests on a heel tip with an area of 0.00010 m². What pressure does the heel exert?

whyNot.2: Off by a factor of 100 in dividing by 0.00010.
whyNot.3: Gives the force value; it must be divided by the tiny area.

explain.body: P = ρgh is directly proportional to depth: triple the depth, triple the extra pressure.

test.q: The extra water pressure 10 m below the surface of a lake is about 100 kPa. About what is the extra pressure at 30 m?
test.why: P = ρgh is proportional to depth: three times as deep gives three times the extra pressure, 300 kPa.

whyNot.0: Squares the depth factor; pressure is linear in depth.
whyNot.2: Pressure grows with depth; it does not stay the same.
whyNot.3: Divides instead of multiplying; deeper means more pressure.

explain.body: The upward push of a fluid equals the weight of the fluid the object displaces.

test.q: What does the buoyant force on a fully submerged object equal?
options: The object's volume times its density
The weight of the fluid it displaces
The density of the surrounding fluid
test.why: Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = weight of the fluid displaced.

whyNot.0: That holds only for a floating object at rest, not every submerged one.
whyNot.1: Volume × the object's density is its mass; the fluid's properties set buoyancy.
whyNot.3: Density alone is not a force; the displaced volume and g also matter.
